# CPU features

@difference Extension: the runtime finds out which optional CPU instruction sets exist, and the environment variable `BLITZLLVM_CPU` lowers what it may use.

Programs are compiled for the generic target of their architecture: x86-64 with SSE2, or ARMv8.0 with NEON on arm64. The runtime does not assume anything beyond that. It asks the CPU once, when the first part of it needs the answer (`cpuid` and `xgetbv` on x86, which also makes sure the operating system saves the wide registers; `getauxval` on arm64 Linux, `sysctl` on macOS and `IsProcessorFeaturePresent` on arm64 Windows), and code that is faster with an optional instruction set only runs when the CPU has it.

`BLITZLLVM_CPU` lowers the result, which is how each of those code paths is tested without owning every CPU. It never adds a feature the CPU does not have. It holds a list, separated by commas:

| Setting | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `baseline` | No optional features: SSE2 only on x86-64, NEON only on arm64. |
| `v2`, `v3`, `v4` | x86-64 only: at most the features of the x86-64-v2, -v3 or -v4 microarchitecture level (v4 is AVX-512). |
| `native` | What the CPU has. This is the default. |
| `-<feature>` | Removes a feature and everything that needs it, such as `-avx2`, `-fma`, `-sse4.1`, `-dotprod` or `-sve2`. |

For example `BLITZLLVM_CPU=v3,-fma` runs as an AVX2 machine without FMA. A program started with `--profile` and `BLITZ_FPS=1` prints the result as `cpu: x86_64 v3: sse3 ssse3 ...` before the first frame report. Which features are used, and where, can differ between versions.
